extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and critics of poetry (particularly Romantic/Wordsworthian criticism)
extracted.subtask_description: A close-critical framework for judging the aesthetic qualities of Wordsworth's poems (and poetic works of similar temper)—listing characteristic virtues and defects such as thought, diction, imagery, pathos, imagination, and audience‑fit, illustrated with textual examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence on youth and practical moral instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: How much warmer the interest is, how much more genial the feelings of reality and practicability, and thence how much stronger the impulses to imitation are, which a contemporary writer, and especially a contemporary poet, excites in youth and commencing manhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise is due to exertion of such influence; a contemporary poet who teaches the young mind to think well and wisely by natural processes does important social work. (Author applies this praise to Wordsworth.) No specimen quotations given here; point used as a justificatory criterion of value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondent weight and sanity of Thoughts and Sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A correspondent weight and sanity of the Thoughts and Sentiments,—won, not from books; but—from the poet’s own meditative observation. They are fresh and have the dew upon them. His muse... makes audible a linked lay of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valued when thoughts arise from personal meditation rather than mere learning; freshness and originality of reflection count highly. Examples are cited (several quatrains, sonnets, and passages) to show just and original reflection making poems valuable. Comparison to Samuel Daniel: sentiments that retain freshness on repeated reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeless diction (diction bears no mark of time)
rubrics_metrics.description: His diction bears no mark of time, no distinction of age which has been, and as long as our language shall last, will be so far the language of the to-day and for ever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction that remains intelligible and unaffected by transitory fashions is a positive quality. The critic notes that Wordsworth’s diction and sentiments resist deterioration through frequent perusal and remain fresh to readers across ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspicuity to intended readers (fit audience find, though few)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem is not necessarily obscure, because it does not aim to be popular. It is enough, if a work be perspicuous to those for whom it is written, and 'Fit audience find, though few.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepts some difficulty or limited intelligibility for general readers so long as the intended, habituated audience can understand; the Ode on Intimations of Immortality is cited as 'arduous and high' but plain enough for readers accustomed to introspective observation. Anti‑pattern: expecting universal popularity/intelligibility as sole test of merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sinewy strength and originality of single lines and paragraphs (curiosa felicitas)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sinewy strength and originality of single lines and paragraphs: the frequent curiosa felicitas of his diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual lines or short passages that show concentrated power and felicitous diction are an important metric; even detractors acknowledge this quality. The critic treats such singular felicities as a distinguishing excellence deserving citation (though specimens are said to be elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect truth of nature in images and descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfect truth of nature in his images and descriptions as taken immediately from nature, and proving a long and genial intimacy with the very spirit which gives the physiognomic expression to all the works of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Images should be faithful to observed nature yet elevated—"distinguished from the reality only by [their] greater softness and lustre." Examples given: skating passage (vol. I pp. 42–47), 'The Green Linnet', descriptions of the blue-cap, noontide silence, cuckoo poem, etc. Value attributed where poet brings out subtle veins and tints overlooked by ordinary observation; anti‑pattern: distortion or false‑colouring of objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meditative pathos and contemplative sympathy with man
rubrics_metrics.description: A meditative pathos, a union of deep and subtle thought with sensibility; a sympathy with man as man; the sympathy indeed of a contemplator, rather than a fellow‑sufferer or co‑mate... the Man and the Poet lose and find themselves in each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contemplative sympathy allows the poet to perceive a 'human face divine' beneath suffering or ignorance; it produces affecting work (the critic cites 'The Affliction of Margaret', 'The Mad Mother', etc., as instances that move readers to tears). The poet’s stance is more observant and philosophic than merely commiserative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gift of Imagination (highest and strictest sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: I challenge for this poet the gift of Imagination in the highest and strictest sense of the word... In imaginative power, he stands nearest of all modern writers to Shakespeare and Milton; and yet in a kind perfectly unborrowed and his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination here is the supreme faculty: the power to 'add the gleam, The light that never was, on sea or land,' i.e., to consecrate and transform perception. The critic notes that Wordsworth's fancy may sometimes be awkward or recondite, but his deeper imaginative power is pre‑eminent; many passages (e.g., Yew Trees, Resolution and Independence, sonnets, 'Ode') are cited as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between fancy and imagination; accept uneven fancy
rubrics_metrics.description: His fancy seldom displays itself, as mere and unmodified fancy. But in imaginative power, he stands nearest to Shakespeare and Milton... The likeness is occasionally too strange, or demands too peculiar a point of view, or is such as appears the creature of predetermined research, rather than spontaneous presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that felicitous imagination can coexist with occasional awkwardness of fancy: evaluators should separate transient lapses of fancifulness from the deeper, higher faculty of imagination. Anti‑pattern: rejecting a poet wholesale for occasional peculiar or recondite figures of fancy.
